lead: An avionics box must work in a hot, vibrating bay full of electrical noise. Packaging fixes its shape and connectors so a line replaceable unit (LRU) can be swapped on the ramp. Cooling carries its heat to air or liquid. Electromagnetic interference and compatibility (EMI/EMC) rules limit what the box emits and what it must tolerate. Some syllabi leave this chapter out; the same ideas apply to every avionics box on every aircraft.
prereq: You need first-year heat transfer (thermal resistance); no earlier chapter is required, though 3.1 shows where the supply comes from.

blocks.text: An LRU is a box that can be removed and replaced as one unit without opening it. It slides into a rack or a front-loading tray. Hold-down clamps lock it against vibration. Blind connectors at the rear mate when the tray is pushed home, so no hand tools are needed on the ramp.

Civil cases follow ARINC 404, whose air transport rack (ATR) sizes run from ¼ ATR to 1 ATR, or the newer ARINC 600, whose sizes are counted in modular concept units (MCU). These standards fix case dimensions, connector positions and the cooling-air interface, so boxes from different makers fit the same rack. Military (DOD) types use similar ideas with harsher environmental limits. Weight and volume matter because every kilogram costs fuel; access matters because a faulty box must come out in minutes. The connector carries power and signals. Keying prevents a wrong box from entering a tray. The case also provides the shield and the heat path, so its metalwork is part of both the electrical and thermal design.

Every watt lost as heat raises temperature. Natural convection suits small boxes. Larger bays use forced air, a cold plate, or a liquid loop. A cold plate is a metal plate with internal passages; the LRU mounts flat on it and heat flows by conduction. Liquid loops carry heat to a fuel-cooled or air-cooled heat exchanger. Cold-plate mounting needs a flat, clamped surface; a poor contact adds resistance.
Thermal resistance R<sub>th</sub> is the temperature rise per watt, in kelvin per watt (K/W). For one path:

blocks.where: T<sub>case</sub> is case temperature in °C; T<sub>air</sub> is cooling-air inlet temperature in °C; P is heat in W; R<sub>th</sub> is case-to-air resistance in K/W.

blocks.text: Inside the box, each hot component has its own junction-to-case resistance R<sub>jc</sub>: T<sub>j</sub> = T<sub>case</sub> + P<sub>device</sub> × R<sub>jc</sub>, where P<sub>device</sub> is the heat of that one component, not of the whole LRU. The real limit is the hottest semiconductor junction, not the box surface. Less airflow raises R<sub>th</sub>; in forced-air cooling halving the flow can come close to doubling it, so the same power gives a hotter case. Worked example 2 follows the heat from the case to a chip.

EMI is unwanted electromagnetic energy, carried as current along a wire or as a field through space, that disturbs equipment. EMC means the box works in that environment without disturbing others. Conducted emission travels along wires; radiated emission travels through space. Susceptibility is how easily the box is upset, by conducted or radiated energy.

Four controls work together. Suppress at the source with filters and ferrites. Route signals as screened twisted pairs and keep power cables away from signal cables. Screened means a conductive layer around the pair; twisted means the two wires swap positions along the run, so pickup cancels. Filter at the connector with feed-through capacitors. Shield the enclosure with conductive gaskets, then bond it to the airframe with a low-impedance path. Bonding is a direct metal connection; grounding is the reference return.
RTCA DO-160 covers environmental and EMI tests; MIL-STD-461 covers military EMI. The box must pass both emission and susceptibility limits. A shield with a poor bond is an antenna.

examples.question: An LRU dissipates 120 W. Its cold plate has a thermal resistance of 0.15 K/W to the cooling air, and the inlet air is at 30 °C. (a) Find the case temperature. (b) The airflow is halved and the resistance doubles; the case limit is 70 °C. Is there still margin?
steps: Given P = 120 W, R<sub>th</sub> = 0.15 K/W, T<sub>air</sub> = 30 °C.
examples.answer: The case temperature is 48 °C; with halved airflow it is 66 °C, leaving 4 °C of margin.

examples.question: In the 66 °C case of Worked example 1(b), a power transistor dissipates 5 W and has a junction-to-case resistance of 2.0 K/W. Its junction limit is 125 °C, and the designer wants at least 40 K of margin. Is the design acceptable?
steps: Use the device's own heat: P<sub>device</sub> = 5 W (not the 120 W of the whole LRU).
Rise from case to junction = 5 × 2.0 = 10 K.
Margin = 125 − 76 = 49 K, which is more than the 40 K wanted.
At full airflow the case is 48 °C, so T<sub>j</sub> = 48 + 10 = 58 °C and the margin is 67 K.
examples.answer: Yes: the junction reaches 76 °C with halved airflow, a margin of 49 K; at full airflow it is 58 °C.

traps: Bench pass does not guarantee bay pass: reduced airflow raises R<sub>th</sub> and the case temperature.
Conducted emission leaves through wires; radiated emission leaves through air. Do not swap the words.
Temperature rise is P × R<sub>th</sub>, not R<sub>th</sub> ÷ P; use W and K/W to get K.
Shielding alone is not EMC; a poor bond, unfiltered connector or badly routed power cable still fails.
Using the whole LRU power with R<sub>jc</sub>. The junction rise uses the heat of that one device.

quiz.a: A line replaceable unit: a box removable and replaceable as one unit on the ramp.
It gives a low-resistance conduction path from the case to air or liquid.

quiz.q: An LRU dissipates 80 W; R<sub>th</sub> = 0.20 K/W; air is 25 °C. Find the case temperature.
Why can bench EMC pass fail in the aircraft?
quiz.a: Long cables, poor bonds, gaskets and nearby transmitters change both paths.
Conducted travels along wires; radiated travels through air.

quiz.q: Why bond an enclosure to the airframe?
quiz.a: Bonding gives interference currents and fault currents a low-impedance path to the airframe, so the case does not float at a noise voltage and the shield works; a poorly bonded shield acts as an antenna. It also protects people from shock and limits lightning damage.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern designs use liquid-cooled cold plates and additive-manufactured heat sinks to lower the same thermal resistance. Fibre-optic links avoid conducted interference. Search next for cold plate thermal resistance, DO-160, MIL-STD-461 and EMI gasket bonding.

figure.caption: The heat path of the worked examples. With full airflow the 120 W LRU sits 18 K above the 30 °C air (case 48 °C) and the 5 W chip 10 K above that; halving the airflow doubles the rise to 36 K (case 66 °C, 4 K under its limit; junction 76 °C).
